discussion_comments.comment_body:
For each intercepted assignment, we clear and rebuild the whole map with n entries and p assignments. This is O(np) work with a worse case O(n²) if p scales with n.

Could we write tests for Map and Set payloads with many deferred references?

In the PR description you write:
> Returns null on cycle detection to indicate "no I/O found on this cyclic path" (not undefined, which would signal abort semantics and skip emitting I/O info for other non-cyclic branches)

However, this doesn't actually fix the reported issue. I've synced your fix to the repro app and it still runs into a stack overflow. The fix just appears to work because it's not applied correctly here:

https://github.com/jere-co/next-debug/blob/25c992b4e021765343067a30d8b70fa20a337448/patch-visitAsyncNode.cjs#L128

That patch returns `undefined` instead of `null`. If we did that, we'd drop I/O info for valid cases, which you can see with the failing unit tests that this change would trigger.

Also, I think the `IN_PROGRESS` sentinel as implemented here doesn't actually change the cycle detection behavior. The original code already returns `null` for a cycle (via `visited.get(node)` returning the `null` that was set before recursing). The sentinel would only matter if we wanted to return something _different_ on cycle detection.

It seems like the DB library is producing very long linear chains of async nodes via `previous` pointers, and the stack overflow comes from the recursive traversal of these chains, not from undetected cycles. A proper fix might require converting the `previous` chain traversal from recursive to iterative, though this gets complicated because the traversal also needs to handle `awaited` branches and return values need to propagate correctly.

Instead of recursively traversing the fiber tree, you could dispatch a separate "toggleStrictMode" action for each child. This would be more consistent with how other actions are handled in the codebase.

We should try to avoid recursion when not necessary. For example, a pattern we typically use is check if something is resolved first and then initialize and then check if something is initialized instead of a single switch.

In this case, there can also be a lot of listeners when there's a lot of references to the same thing so in theory you can actually stack overflow because of this recursion.

Instead, you should check if the status has changed to initialized or errored here and if so call `wakeChunk` or `rejectChunk` respectively.
